samples.text:
The bar chart shows how much money households in five income groups spend on energy every week, and the table shows how much energy each group use and what percentage of their income they spend on it.

Overall, richer households spend more money and use more energy, but the poorer households spend bigger part of their income on energy.

According to the bar chart, the lowest 20% spend $28 per week on energy. The second group spend $33 and the middle group spend $37. The fourth group spend $42 and the highest 20% spend the most, $55 per week, which is almost double of the lowest group.

In the table, the energy used also increase with income. The lowest group use 9,800 kWh per year, and the number goes up to 11,400, 12,900 and 14,700 kWh. The highest group use 19,200 kWh. However, the percentage of income is opposite. The lowest group spend 11.2% of their income on energy, but the second group spend 7.5% and the middle group 5.4%. The fourth group spend 4.1% and the highest group spend only 2.9%.
samples.why: Relevant overview identifying the main contrast · all figures accurate but listed mechanically · repetitive structures (The ... group spend) · limited vocabulary · errors in articles, agreement and phrasing.

samples.text:
The bar chart illustrates the average amount that households in five income groups spend on energy each week, while the table provides information on their annual energy consumption and the proportion of their income that goes on energy.

Overall, both spending on energy and energy use rise steadily with income. However, the poorest households devote a far larger share of their income to energy than the wealthiest ones.

Weekly spending ranges from $28 for the lowest 20% of earners to $55 for the highest 20%, so the richest group spends almost twice as much. The increases between the lower groups are fairly even, at around $4–5 each, whereas the gap between the fourth and highest groups is much wider, at $13.

A similar pattern can be seen in energy use. The lowest-income households consume 9,800 kWh a year, which rises to 14,700 kWh for the fourth group and 19,200 kWh for the top group. In contrast, the percentage of income spent on energy falls sharply as incomes rise. It stand at 11.2% for the poorest fifth, compared with 7.5% for the second group and 5.4% for the middle group, and drops to only 2.9% among the richest households.
samples.why: Clear overview of the central contrast · key features highlighted with useful differences · good range of cohesive devices · some less common vocabulary (devote, consumption) · mostly error-free with one slip.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares average weekly energy expenditure across five household income groups, and the table details each group's annual energy consumption together with the share of income that this spending represents.

Wealthier households both spend more on energy and use more of it, yet energy costs place a far heavier burden on lower-income households, for whom they absorb a much larger proportion of earnings.

Weekly spending climbs steadily through the income bands, from $28 for the lowest fifth to $42 for the fourth, before jumping to $55 for the top fifth, almost double the figure for the poorest group. Energy consumption follows the same upward gradient: the lowest-income households use 9,800 kWh annually, while the highest-income households use 19,200 kWh, again nearly twice as much.

The relationship reverses, however, when spending is viewed as a percentage of income. The poorest fifth of households devote 11.2% of their income to energy, around four times the proportion spent by the richest fifth (2.9%). Between these extremes, the figure declines progressively, from 7.5% for the second group to 5.4% for the middle group and 4.1% for the fourth.
samples.why: Well-judged overview capturing the inverse relationship · figures selected purposefully with accurate multiples · skilful cohesion across both visuals · precise vocabulary (burden, gradient, absorb) · varied, error-free structures.
